w: Ring after ring of fortification, thrown up over centuries to guard the old maritime republic's capital: Genoa still holds more city wall, and longer stretches of it, than any other city in Italy. Great chunks survive today, climbing the hills behind the port like a stone spine over the city.
s: More surviving city wall than anywhere else in Italy
_facts: several circles of walls that protected Genoa, former capital of the Republic of Genoa
large portions remain to this day
Genoa has more and longer walls than any other city in Italy

w: On 14 August 2018 a 210-metre span of Riccardo Morandi's 1960s viaduct gave way in a rainstorm, killing 43 people and tipping the whole region into a year-long state of emergency. The wreckage was cleared by 2019; the Genoa-Saint George Bridge now spans the same valley in its place.
s: The bridge that fell, and the one that rose after it
_facts: cable-stayed viaduct built 1963-67 over the Polcevera River, connecting Sampierdarena and Cornigliano
designed by engineer Riccardo Morandi
a 210m section collapsed on 14 August 2018, killing 43 people
remains demolished June 2019; replacement Genoa-Saint George Bridge inaugurated a year later

w: Consecrated in 1118 by a pope who died that same year, Genoa's cathedral took two more centuries to finish: Romanesque side naves, a Gothic facade thrown up in the 1200s, then a dome and bell tower bolted on in the 1500s. Seat of the Archbishop of Genoa ever since, in one long, mismatched climb toward heaven.
s: A cathedral built across three different centuries
_facts: consecrated by Pope Gelasius II in 1118
built 12th-14th century; Romanesque naves, Gothic facade from the early 1200s
bell tower and dome added in the 16th century
seat of the Archbishop of Genoa

w: Genoa's grand civic square, built around a fountain the Genoese never tire of photographing. At the end of the 19th century this was the financial engine room of the whole country: stock exchange, Credito Italiano, a Bank of Italy branch, so locals still nickname it 'the City,' a nod to its own square mile.
s: Where Genoa once played banker to all of Italy
_facts: main square of Genoa, known for its restored fountain
surrounded by banks, insurers and office buildings; nicknamed the 'City' of Genoa
late 19th century Genoa was Italy's main financial centre alongside Milan
stock exchange, Credito Italiano and a Bank of Italy branch were established here

w: Rebuilt to its current shape in 1543, La Lanterna guided ships into the port of Genoa for 359 years as the tallest lighthouse on Earth before a French rival edged it out. At 76 metres it is still the tallest lighthouse in Italy and the whole Mediterranean, and the oldest, proudest symbol the city has.
s: The tower that was the world's tallest lighthouse
_facts: main light for the Port of Genoa, symbol and landmark of the city
rebuilt to its current form in 1543; world's fourth oldest lighthouse
76m tall; was the world's tallest lighthouse from 1543 until 1902
still the tallest lighthouse in Italy and the Mediterranean

w: Long before Venice cornered the branding, Genoa had its own doges, and this was their palace, with two grand faces looking onto two different squares. These days it trades power for culture, hosting exhibitions and cultural events where the republic's rulers once ran the business of a maritime empire.
s: Where Genoa's own doges once held court
_facts: historical building once home to the Doges of Genoa
now a museum and centre for cultural events and arts exhibitions
two entrances/facades: main on Piazza Giacomo Matteotti, second on Piazza De Ferrari

w: Spread across a hillside above the city, Staglieno is less a cemetery than an open-air sculpture gallery, one of the largest burial grounds in Europe, famous for the sheer theatrical grief carved into its monuments. Visitors and art historians alike come to wander among the marble angels rather than to mourn.
s: A square kilometre of marble grief, sculpted
_facts: monumental cemetery on a hillside in the Staglieno district
famous for its monumental sculpture
covers more than a square kilometre; one of the largest cemeteries in Europe

w: Genoa's aristocracy built this 'new street' during the Renaissance purely to show off, lining it with palazzi grand enough that it and its neighbours earned UNESCO World Heritage status in 2006 as the Strade Nuove and the Palazzi dei Rolli. Old money, still unapologetically on display.
s: A Renaissance street built to out-flex Genoa's rivals
_facts: historic street known for its ancient palaces
one of the Strade Nuove built by Genoese aristocracy during the Renaissance
inscribed since July 2006 as part of the UNESCO World Heritage listing for Genoa

w: Genoa's principal opera house stands just off Piazza De Ferrari, in the thick of the city's civic heart. It's still the address for opera, ballet, orchestral concerts and recitals alike, the grand room the city built for the nights it wanted velvet seats instead of a working port.
s: Genoa's grand stage, a few steps off the main square
_facts: principal opera house of Genoa
used for opera, ballet, orchestral music and recitals
located on the side of Piazza De Ferrari

w: Set on the hills of Carignano just above the old centre, this Renaissance church has lent its neighbourhood a second name: most Genoese just call it Santa Maria Assunta di Carignano. A quiet perch with a view over the rooftops it was built to watch.
s: A Renaissance church that gave a hillside its nickname
_facts: Renaissance church in Genoa, located in the Carignano district on the hills above the centre
also known as Santa Maria Assunta di Carignano

w: Built in the 1700s as the 'Strada Nuovissima,' the newest of the new streets, Via Cairoli later took the name of Benedetto Cairoli, Italy's tenth prime minister. Like its sister streets nearby, it made the UNESCO list in 2006 as part of the Strade Nuove and the Palazzi dei Rolli.
s: The newest of Genoa's historic 'new streets'
_facts: street in the historical centre named after PM Benedetto Cairoli (1825-1889)
built in the 18th century as 'Strada Nuovissima'
one of the Strade Nuove inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage list in July 2006

w: Consecrated in 1189 and rebuilt more than once since, including after a 1684 naval bombardment, this Romanesque church still holds serious treasure inside: a 1515 triptych by the Flemish master Joos van Cleve and a Madonna by Nicolo da Voltri. A small church with an outsized art collection.
s: A 12th-century church that survived a naval bombardment
_facts: 12th-century Romanesque church, consecrated 1 May 1189
restored after the 1684 bombardment of Genoa, reconsecrated 1892
interior holds a Madonna by Nicolo da Voltri, a St Joseph by Domenico Piola
1515 triptych (Adoration of the Magi) by Joos van Cleve

w: Built in 1560 for the nobleman Tobia Pallavicino, this villa once stood entirely outside Genoa's walls, until the 19th-century city simply grew around it and swallowed it into Castelletto. Remarkably, more than four and a half centuries on, it still belongs to the Pallavicino family.
s: A 1560s villa still owned by the family that built it
_facts: 16th-century villa built 1560 for nobleman Tobia Pallavicino
originally outside the city walls; now in the Castelletto quarter after 19th-century expansion
still belongs to the Pallavicino family

n: Shrine of Nostra Signora della Guardia
w: Perched atop Monte Figogna, where medieval lookouts once tracked armies moving through the valley below, this is Liguria's most important Marian shrine, and, on a clear day, you can supposedly see all the way to Corsica from its steps. Pilgrims still climb up from Genoa and beyond to reach it.
s: A mountaintop shrine with a view clear to Corsica
_facts: Roman Catholic pilgrimage site atop Monte Figogna (804m), most important Marian shrine in Liguria
medieval strategic observation post for the Polcevera valley and approaches to Genoa
on a clear day the mountains of Corsica are visible from the shrine
destination of pilgrims from Genoa and across Italy
